title: Chart Types
summary: Build bar, line, and pie charts from Orders data to visualise comparisons, trends, and part-of-whole shares.

steps.title: Bar Charts: Comparing Categories
steps.lede: A bar chart places categories on one axis and values on the other to show comparisons at a glance.

blocks.text: Bar charts illustrate comparisons among individual items; in a bar chart, the categories are typically organised along one axis and the values along the other. A summary table of total order amount by city is exactly the kind of category-versus-value data a bar chart compares.

To create a chart, select the data, choose Insert > Recommended Charts, and select a chart on the Recommended Charts tab to preview it. If you don't see a bar chart you like, select the All Charts tab to see all chart types, select the chart, and click OK.

blocks.caption: City order totals — source data for a bar chart. Each city is a category; total_amount is the value.

steps.title: Building a Bar Chart in Excel
steps.lede: See how to select data and insert a bar chart from the Charts group.

segments.label: Selecting data and inserting a column/bar chart from the Charts group
segments.summary: The presenter highlights a monthly sales table, opens the Insert tab, and picks a 2-D column chart directly from the Charts gallery. After inserting, they explore chart style options and the Switch Row/Column toggle to flip which dimension appears on each axis. They then use the chart's filter to remove a totals row and a year-end total column that were distorting the scale, apply the change, and add a title. The finished chart shows months along the horizontal axis and bar heights representing product quantities, making it easy to see that paper is the top-selling product every month.

segments.label: Insert > Column Chart button: selecting data and fixing category order
segments.summary: Starting from a selected data range, the presenter goes to the Insert tab, clicks the Column Chart button, and chooses the bar chart option. They immediately notice that the category axis lists items in the reverse of the source data order. To fix this, they select the axis, press Ctrl+1 to open Format Axis, and check 'Categories in reverse order', restoring the original top-to-bottom sequence from the data.

steps.title: Building a Bar Chart from Category Data
steps.lede: Test your understanding of bar chart axis encoding and the Insert > Recommended Charts workflow.

public.prompt: You have a table with two columns: city and total_amount. You want to create a bar chart to compare total order amounts across cities. Which axis encoding is correct for a bar chart?

options.text: Cities on the category axis; total_amount values represented by bar lengths on the value axis.
total_amount values on the category axis; cities represented by bar lengths on the value axis.
Cities on both axes, with total_amount shown as a colour gradient.
total_amount on both axes, with cities shown as data labels inside the bars.

opt_b.message: In a bar chart, categories (like city names) go on the category axis, and numeric values (like total_amount) are represented by bar lengths on the value axis — not the other way around.

opt_c.message: Bar charts do not use colour gradients to encode values. The category axis holds the category labels (cities) and the value axis holds the numeric values (total_amount), shown as bar lengths.

opt_d.message: Both axes cannot hold the same type of data. The category axis holds category labels (cities) and the value axis holds numeric values (total_amount) represented by bar lengths.

correct.message: Correct! In a bar chart, categories (city names) are organised along the category axis and numeric values (total_amount) are represented by bar lengths along the value axis.

incorrect.message: In a bar chart, categories go on the category axis and numeric values are shown as bar lengths on the value axis. Cities are the categories; total_amount is the value.

hints: A bar chart compares items: the items (categories) go on one axis, and their values (shown as bar lengths) go on the other.
Ask yourself: what am I comparing? Those are the categories. What am I measuring? That is the value axis.

steps.title: Build a Bar Chart from City Totals
steps.lede: Select the city totals table and insert a bar chart using Insert > Recommended Charts.

public.prompt: The city_totals sheet has city names in column A (A2:A7) and total order amounts in column B (B2:B7). A bar chart of this data would place cities on the category axis and total amounts as bar lengths on the value axis. In cell C1, write a formula that returns the sum of all total_amount values in B2:B7 — the grand total that would appear in the chart's data range.

correct.message: Correct! =SUM(B2:B7) returns 99300 — the grand total of all city amounts. The bar chart would use B2:B7 as its value data, with each city's bar length proportional to its share of this total.

incorrect.message: Use SUM with the total_amount range: =SUM(B2:B7). The city_totals sheet has 6 cities in rows 2 through 7.

hints: The total_amount values are in column B, rows 2 through 7 (one row per city).
=SUM(B2:B7) adds up all six city totals.

steps.title: Line Charts: Showing Trends Over Time
steps.lede: A line chart distributes evenly-spaced time intervals along the horizontal axis and values along the vertical axis.

blocks.text: In a line chart, category data is distributed evenly along the horizontal axis and value data along the vertical axis. Line charts can show continuous data over time on an evenly scaled axis, making them well suited to showing trends at equal intervals such as months, quarters, or fiscal years. A summary of total order amount by month is exactly this kind of evenly-spaced, time-ordered data.

To create a line chart, select the data, choose Insert > Recommended Charts, and select a chart on the Recommended Charts tab to preview it. If you don't see a line chart you like, select the All Charts tab to see all chart types, select the chart, and click OK.

blocks.caption: Monthly order totals — source data for a line chart. Each month is evenly spaced on the horizontal axis; total_amount maps to the vertical axis.

steps.title: Building a Line Chart from Monthly Sales Data
steps.lede: See how to assign the data range and set the horizontal-axis labels.

segments.label: Inserting a line chart and assigning the data range
segments.summary: The instructor starts with a single-row sales table spanning October through June, with monthly columns. From the Insert menu, Recommended Charts is opened and a 2D line chart with markers is chosen — noting that 3D variants should be avoided. Because no data was selected beforehand, a blank chart appears; right-clicking inside it and choosing Select Data lets the instructor drag cells A1 through J3 as the chart range. The series name and its y-axis values are confirmed, then the horizontal-axis label range is narrowed from B1:J2 down to B2:J2 to remove a two-level header and show only the month names. Clicking OK produces the finished chart.

steps.title: Axis Roles and Interval Suitability
steps.lede: Test your understanding of which axis carries time intervals and when a line chart is appropriate.

public.prompt: Which of the following datasets is best suited for a line chart, and why?

options.text: Monthly revenue totals for Jan through Jun 2024 — because the data is time-ordered at equal intervals, making a line chart ideal for showing the trend.
Total order amounts by city — because cities are categories and a line chart connects them with a line.
A single order's delivery time — because a line chart can show a single data point.
Driver names and their order counts — because a line chart works for any two-column dataset.

opt_b.message: Cities are unordered categories, not time-ordered intervals. A line connecting unordered categories implies a trend that does not exist. A bar chart is better for comparing city totals.

opt_c.message: A single data point cannot show a trend. Line charts are suited to continuous data over time at equal intervals — multiple points that form a meaningful sequence.

opt_d.message: Driver names are unordered categories, not time-ordered intervals. Connecting them with a line would imply a trend that does not exist. A bar chart is more appropriate.

correct.message: Correct! Monthly revenue at equal time intervals (Jan, Feb, Mar…) is exactly the kind of data a line chart is designed for — it shows the trend across evenly spaced time points.

incorrect.message: Line charts are suited to continuous data over time at equal intervals (months, quarters, years). Unordered categories like cities or driver names should use a bar chart instead.

hints: Ask: is the horizontal axis a time sequence with equal spacing? If yes, a line chart works well.
A line connecting unordered categories (like cities) implies a trend that does not exist — that is a misuse of a line chart.

steps.title: Building a Line Chart from Time-Ordered Data
steps.lede: Apply your knowledge of axis encoding and the Recommended Charts workflow.

public.prompt: You have monthly revenue data: month labels in column A (Jan-2024 through Jun-2024) and total amounts in column B. You create a line chart using Insert > Recommended Charts. Which statement correctly describes the resulting chart?

options.text: Month labels are distributed evenly along the horizontal axis; revenue values are plotted on the vertical axis, connected by a line showing the trend over time.
Revenue values are distributed along the horizontal axis; month labels appear on the vertical axis.
Both axes show revenue values; month labels appear as data point labels on the line.
The chart shows bars instead of a line because monthly data always produces a bar chart.

opt_b.message: In a line chart, category data (month labels) is distributed along the horizontal axis and value data (revenue) is plotted on the vertical axis — not the other way around.

opt_c.message: The horizontal axis holds category data (month labels), not revenue values. Revenue values are plotted on the vertical axis.

opt_d.message: Monthly data does not automatically produce a bar chart. When you select the data and use Insert > Recommended Charts, Excel recommends a line chart for evenly spaced time-series data.

correct.message: Correct! In a line chart, category data (month labels) is distributed evenly along the horizontal axis and value data (revenue) is plotted on the vertical axis, with points connected by a line.

incorrect.message: In a line chart, the horizontal axis holds the category data (month labels) evenly spaced, and the vertical axis holds the value data (revenue). The line connects the data points to show the trend.

hints: Remember: horizontal axis = category data (months); vertical axis = value data (revenue).
The line connects the data points in order, showing how revenue changes from month to month.

steps.title: Build a Line Chart from Monthly Totals
steps.lede: Select the monthly summary table and insert a line chart using Insert > Recommended Charts.

public.prompt: The monthly_summary sheet has month labels in column A (A2:A7, Jan-2024 through Jun-2024) and total order amounts in column B (B2:B7). A line chart of this data would place months evenly along the horizontal axis and revenue values on the vertical axis. In cell C1, write a formula that returns the sum of all monthly totals in B2:B7 — the grand total across all six months.

correct.message: Correct! =SUM(B2:B7) returns 1976900 — the total revenue across all six months. The line chart would use B2:B7 as its value data, with each month's point plotted on the vertical axis.

incorrect.message: Use SUM with the total_amount range: =SUM(B2:B7). The monthly_summary sheet has 6 months in rows 2 through 7. To create a line chart from this data, select A1:B7, then go to Insert → Recommended Charts and choose the Line chart option.

hints: The total_amount values are in column B, rows 2 through 7 (one row per month).
=SUM(B2:B7) adds up all six monthly totals.

steps.title: Pie Charts: Part-of-Whole Shares
steps.lede: A pie chart shows each category's share of a total — but only when the data meets four conditions.

blocks.text: Pie charts show the size of items in one data series proportional to the sum of the items. They are appropriate when you have only one data series to plot, none of the values are negative, there are no more than seven categories, and the categories represent parts of the whole pie. A summary of total order amount by city, for no more than seven cities, fits that description as long as no amount is negative.

To create a pie chart, select the data, choose Insert > Recommended Charts, and select a chart on the Recommended Charts tab to preview it. If you don't see a pie chart you like, select the All Charts tab to see all chart types, select the chart, and click OK.

blocks.title: Total Order Amount by City (NGN)
blocks.alt_text: Pie chart showing six slices, one per city. Lagos is the largest slice, followed by Abuja, Port Harcourt, Kano, Ibadan, and Enugu. Each slice is labelled with the city name and its share of total order amount.

steps.title: When a Pie Chart Works: Proportional Slices
steps.lede: See how even-split versus clear-winner data affects whether a pie chart communicates clearly.

segments.label: Pie chart as part-of-whole: even-split versus clear-winner examples
segments.summary: A pie chart displays each category's share of a total, where all slices together represent 100%. The presenter contrasts two scenarios: an 'even split' chart where slices are nearly equal and the story is hard to read, versus a 'clear winner' chart where grouping categories into two or three slices makes one dominant share immediately obvious. The even-split example is also shown remade as a bar chart to illustrate when ranking matters more than part-of-whole. The clear-winner examples show how reducing and grouping categories sharpens the message.

steps.title: Building a Pie Chart from Category Totals
steps.lede: Test your understanding of pie chart eligibility conditions and the creation workflow.

public.prompt: You have city order totals for 6 cities, all amounts positive. You select the data and use Insert > Recommended Charts to create a pie chart. Which statement correctly describes the resulting chart?

options.text: Each city appears as a slice; each slice's size is proportional to that city's share of the total amount; all slices together represent 100% of total revenue.
Each city appears as a bar; bar lengths represent the city's total amount; the chart shows absolute values, not proportions.
Each city appears as a point on a line; the line shows how city totals change from city to city.
Each city appears as a slice, but slices are equal in size because pie charts do not encode values.

opt_b.message: That describes a bar chart, not a pie chart. A pie chart shows proportions: each slice's size represents that category's share of the whole, and all slices together equal 100%.

opt_c.message: That describes a line chart. A pie chart shows proportions as slices of a circle, not points on a line.

opt_d.message: Pie chart slices are not equal — they are sized proportionally to each category's value. A slice for Lagos (the largest city total) would be larger than a slice for Enugu (the smallest).

correct.message: Correct! In a pie chart, each category is a slice sized proportionally to its share of the total. All slices together represent 100% of the data series.

incorrect.message: A pie chart shows proportions: each slice represents one category's share of the whole, sized proportionally to its value. All slices together equal 100%.

hints: The key word for pie charts is 'proportional' — each slice's size shows that category's fraction of the total.
All slices together must equal 100% of the data series — that is what makes it a 'pie'.

steps.title: Build a Pie Chart from City Totals
steps.lede: Select the city totals table and insert a pie chart using Insert > Recommended Charts.

public.prompt: The city_totals sheet has city names in A2:A7 and total amounts in B2:B7. A pie chart is appropriate here because there is only one data series, all values are positive, and the number of categories does not exceed seven. In cell C1, write a formula that counts the number of city labels in A2:A7 — confirming that the category count is within the pie chart eligibility limit.

correct.message: Correct! =COUNTA(A2:A7) returns 6 — there are 6 cities, which is within the seven-category limit for pie charts. With all positive values and a single data series, this dataset meets all pie chart eligibility conditions.

incorrect.message: Use COUNTA to count the city labels in A2:A7: =COUNTA(A2:A7). COUNTA counts non-empty cells, including text labels.

hints: COUNTA counts all non-empty cells, including text. Use it to count the city names in A2:A7.
The pie chart eligibility rule says no more than seven categories. COUNTA(A2:A7) tells you how many categories there are.

steps.title: Chart Types — Key Points
steps.lede: You can now build bar, line, and pie charts and choose the right type for your data.

blocks.text: Bar charts compare categories: the category axis holds labels and the value axis holds bar heights. Line charts show trends over equal time intervals: months, quarters, or fiscal years go on the horizontal axis and values on the vertical axis. Pie charts show part-of-whole shares and require one data series, no negative values, no more than seven categories, and categories that sum to a meaningful whole. For all three types, select the data and use Insert > Recommended Charts to preview and insert.

remediation_steps.title: Bar Chart Axis Encoding and Creation Steps
remediation_steps.lede: A clear contrast shows which data goes on which axis and how to insert the chart.

blocks.text: In a bar chart, categories go on one axis and values on the other. For the city totals table, city names go on the category axis and total_amount values determine bar height. To insert: select the city and total_amount columns, choose Insert > Recommended Charts, preview the bar chart, and click OK. If the bar chart is not on the Recommended tab, open All Charts, select Bar, and click OK.

remediation_steps.title: Line Chart Axis Roles and When to Use One
remediation_steps.lede: Equal time intervals on the horizontal axis make a line chart the right choice.

blocks.text: In a line chart, category data — typically time labels such as Jan-2024, Feb-2024 — is distributed evenly along the horizontal axis, and value data goes on the vertical axis. Line charts are well suited to data measured at equal intervals: months, quarters, or fiscal years. The monthly summary table has six months at equal intervals, so a line chart shows the trend clearly. A table of city totals is not time-ordered, so a bar chart is more appropriate there.

remediation_steps.title: Pie Chart Eligibility and Creation
remediation_steps.lede: Four conditions must hold before a pie chart is appropriate.

blocks.text: A pie chart is appropriate when: (1) you have only one data series to plot, (2) none of the values are negative, (3) there are no more than seven categories, and (4) the categories represent parts of the whole. The city totals table has six cities (≤ 7), all positive amounts, one series, and the cities together represent all orders — so a pie chart is appropriate. To insert: select the city and total_amount columns, choose Insert > Recommended Charts, preview the pie chart, and click OK.
